source_sentences: 38 • D1D2 hybrid MSNs and primate-expanded interneurons show regional and 39 domain specific organization 40 • Subcellular RNA localization reports soma morphology and projection-inferred 41 signatures.

48 We show region-selective, molecular and spatial diversification of medium-spiny-neuron 49 cell types and multiple non-neuronal populations with distinct molecular identities and 50 spatial localizations.

The literature from both animal models and humans 67 shows that GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs) are the dominant neuronal cell 68 type in the striatum (85–95%) 2-5; MSNs are divided into two major populations: D1-type 69 MSNs, which express the dopamine receptor D1 (DRD1), tachykinin precursor 1 (TAC1), 70 and dynorphin; and D2-type MSNs, which express the dopamine receptor D2 (DRD2), 71 proenkephalin (PENK), and enkephalin 2,3,6.
The nucleus accumbens, located at the ventral extension of the striatum, 79 contains both D1 and D2 MSNs and is further divided into core and shell subregions.

Among these 188 are eight neuronal classes that include caudal and lateral ganglionic eminence 189 (CGE/LGE)-derived GABAergic neurons, which are dominated by medium spiny 190 neurons (MSNs) (Figure S3A).
191 We further examined MSNs – the predominant neuronal population of the striatum that 192 are essential for modulating movement control in the basal ganglia circuit 3.

MSNs 193 segregate into two canonical classes – D1 and D2 MSNs – further subdivided into six 194 major dopaminergic MSN subtypes: STRd D1 Striosome, STRd D1 Matrix, STRv D1, 195 STRd D2 Striosome, STRd D2 Matrix and STRv D2 (dorsal striatum, STRd; ventral 196 striatum, STRv) (Figure 2D-E, Figure S3B).
Specifically, D1 and D2 199 striosomal MSNs are enriched within striosome compartments, whereas D1 and D2 200 matrix MSNs predominate in the surrounding matrix (Figure 2E).
201 The proportion of MSN cell types is largely consistent along the anterior-posterior axis 202 (Figure 2F).
D2 MSNs constitute the largest proportion compared to D1 MSNs 203 (approximately 54 % vs 27 %, respectively).
D1 and D2 MSNs together represent ~83 % 204 of all striatal neurons.

205 Beyond these canonical MSN populations, our analyses uncover spatial distributions of 206 several novel and rare MSN cell types described across species including mouse and 207 non-human primate that are “mixed-identity” neurons that co-express D1- and D2-208 associated gene modules – these neurons are not regionally restricted cell types to 209 discrete striatal or pallidal territories 46-48.

The D1–D2 hybrid (STR D1D2 Hybrid), 210 striosome-matrix hybrid (STRd D2 Hybrid), and D1 NUDAP (Neurochemically Unique 211 Domains in the Accumbens and Putamen) (STRv D1 NUDAP) MSNs are primarily 212 localized within the putamen, caudate nucleus, and nucleus accumbens (Figure 2G), 213 but are largely absent from the globus pallidus and internal capsule.

The mixed state of 214 these cell populations is corroborated by colocalization within individual neurons of 215 multiple transcripts of DRD1, DRD2, and prodynorphin (PDYN), a canonical striosomal 216 MSN marker (Figure 2H).

Cholinergic interneurons and globus pallidus neurons including 275 GPi Core, GPi Shell, CN LHX6–GBX1, and GPe MEIS2–SOX6 populations, exhibit the 276 largest median soma volumes (up to ~9,400 µm³), whereas LAMP5+ interneurons and 277 MSNs display markedly smaller volumes (~1,800 µm³ and ~2,500 µm³, respectively) 278 (Figure 4B).

Although MSN subtypes are more consistent in soma volumes, other 280 neuronal classes exhibit more subtype-dependent variability; for example, SST–CHODL 281 interneurons have among the largest median volumes (~6,200 µm³), while SST–282 ADARB2 interneurons are significantly smaller (~2,300 µm³) (p-value = 6.9 x 10-15, 283 Wilcoxon rank-sum test).

Focusing on MSNs, in the mouse and monkey basal ganglia 288 circuitry, D1 matrix MSNs project directly to the GPi and substantia nigra pars reticulata, 289 whereas D2 matrix MSNs form the indirect pathway via the GPe 3,54.
This might reflect that specific semaphorin 302 gene family members mediate long range connections in neurons such as MSNs 303 targeting specific segments of the globus pallidus 55,57.
Similarly, STRv D1 and STRv D2 MSNs 320 are enriched in the nucleus accumbens shell and core, while STRd D1 and STRd D2 321 MSNs populate the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen) (Figure 5C).
330 Quantitative analysis of MSN subtype proportions across striatal subregions reveals that 331 the caudate nucleus and putamen share comparable D1/D2 ratios (Figure 5C).
In 332 contrast, both D1- and D2-striosomal MSNs are detected in the NAc shell but are 333 largely absent from the NAc core (Figure 5G–H).
To delineate these domains, we 343 further applied cellular community analysis restricted to MSN subtype composition—the 344 principal determinant of striosome–matrix identity (Figure 6A-B).
Beyond canonical 345 D1/D2 MSN distributions, we identify additional cell types exhibiting previously 346 uncharacterized striosome–matrix enrichments.
Orthologous mouse MSNs were 375 identified by correlating gene-expression signatures with human subtypes (Figure S8A, 376 B).
Mouse supertypes 0268 STR D1 GABA_4 and 0267 STR D1 GABA_3 correspond 377 to human STRd D1 Striosome and STRd D1 Matrix MSNs, respectively (Figure S8C–D).

378 Similarly, finer subclustering of the mouse 0277 STR D2 Gaba_4 supertype, designated 379 17 as A* and B*, map to human STRd D2 Striosome MSN and STRd D2 Matrix MSN, 380 respectively (Figure S8E–F).

381 Using these orthologous MSN pairs, we delineated striosome–matrix boundaries in the 382 mouse striatum and performed analogous proximity analyses in which we computed the 383 distance of cells from border of nearest striosome (Figure 6I) and quantified the 384 distribution of cells as a function of distance.
Most gradient-associated transcripts are enriched in lateral ganglionic 440 eminence (CN/LGE)-derived GABAergic neurons, the principal MSN population.

Within the striatum, we map both the most abundant D1 and D2 MSNs 473 into striosome and matrix compartments as well as the less abundant, hybrid-identity 474 MSN cell types (e.g., STR D1D2 Hybrid; STRd D2 Hybrid), and show their preferential 475 localization to the caudate, putamen, and NAc but not to GP or internal capsule.
Within NAc, we uncover that both D1- and 499 D2-striosomal MSNs populate NAc shell but are largely absent in core, consistent with 500 TH (striosome) and KIRREL3 (matrix) compartment markers.
501 The matrix and striosome spatial modules derived from MSN subtype composition 502 reveals fine-scale spatial organization biases.

Cross-species 507 comparison with the MERFISH-derived mouse cell type atlas 10,14 identifies orthologous 508 MSN counterparts (e.g., mouse 0268 D1 and 0267 D1 supertypes corresponding to 509 human STRd D1 striosome and matrix respectively) and confirms border-enriched 510 astrocyte (Astro-TE NN_3) and oligodendrocyte (MOL NN_4) supertypes in mouse.

522 We find that cholinergic interneurons and pallidal neuron subtypes (e.g., GPi Core/Shell; 523 GPe NDB–SI–LHX6/8–GBX1; GPe MEIS2–SOX6) exhibit the largest soma volumes, 524 whereas LAMP5+ interneurons and MSNs are among the smallest.
While the nine 526 MSN subtypes show largely similar volumes, SST+ interneuron subclasses diverge 527 markedly; for example, SST–CHODL versus SST–ADARB2 interneurons show 528 substantial differences.

The main differences were that we only used MSN cell types when building the 1541 cell type composition matrix and we only included the cells in the striatum for the 1542 analysis as the Striosome and Matrix compartments exist only in this part of the Basal 1543 ganglia.

In detail, we first built a K-nearest neighbor graph based on the spatial location 1544 of MSN subtypes using the scikit-learn package82, then we queried the graph to identify 1545 67 50 nearest MSNs for each cell in the striatum.
Next, as explained in 14, we defined the 1546 composition matrix as distance weighted frequency count of neighboring MSN subtypes.
Next, we computed the 1673 differential gene expression between STRd D1 Matrix and STRd D2 matrix MSNs.

The 1674 differential expression was quantified as a difference-in-difference: the deviation of 1675 STRd D1 Matrix MSN’s pseudobulk expression from the across-cell-type mean, minus 1676 the deviation of STRd D2 matrix MSN’s pseudobulk expression from that mean.
Through this approach, 1696 we identified the mouse homologs of the human D1 Matrix and Striosome MSNs.

This is consistent with histological studies in mouse and human basal 279 ganglia 51-53.
These quantitative reconstructions highlight the pronounced 284 morphological diversity among neuronal subtypes in the human basal ganglia.

source_sentences: Analysis of two 218 posterior sections encompassing both internal (GPi) and external (GPe) segments 219 reveal six transcriptionally distinct GP-associated neuronal classes: GPi Shell, GPi Core, 220 GPin-BF Cholinergic, CN LHX6–GBX1, GPe SOX6–CTXND1, and GPe MEIS2–SOX6 221 10 (Figure 2I, Figure S4).
As indicated by their nomenclature, GPi Shell and GPi Core 222 neurons are localized to peripheral and central GP regions, respectively (Figure 2J).

Cholinergic interneurons and globus pallidus neurons including 275 GPi Core, GPi Shell, CN LHX6–GBX1, and GPe MEIS2–SOX6 populations, exhibit the 276 largest median soma volumes (up to ~9,400 µm³), whereas LAMP5+ interneurons and 277 MSNs display markedly smaller volumes (~1,800 µm³ and ~2,500 µm³, respectively) 278 (Figure 4B).
For example, GPe SOX8–CTXND1 and GPe MEIS2–318 SOX6 neurons are enriched in the external globus pallidus (GPe), whereas GPi Core 319 and GPi Shell neurons are confined to the GPi.

Within 476 the globus pallidus, we delineate six GP-associated classes: GPi Shell, GPi Core, GPin-477 BF Cholinergic, CN LHX6–GBX1, GPe SOX6–CTXND1, and GPe MEIS2–SOX6 based 478 on their single-cell transcriptional profiles and reveal their spatial locations within the 479 GPe/GPi shell and core anatomical regions.

source_sentences: Notably, STR TAC3–PLPP4 347 interneurons are exclusively localized to the matrix compartment (Figure 6C, 6D top).
In our human dataset, 350 STR TAC3–PLPP4 neurons are among the most abundant population of striatal 351 interneurons (Figure 6E).

This marked expansion of TAC3–354 PLPP4 interneurons in primates suggests an evolutionary adaptation that supports the 355 integration of the greater density of prefrontal and associative cortical inputs, potentially 356 enabling enhanced sensorimotor and cognitive control 11,65.

The identification of matrix-confined TAC3–PLPP4 interneurons and 390 boundary-enriched glial subtypes further reveals an evolutionarily elaborated 391 compartmental architecture in the human striatum that integrates neuronal and non-392 neuronal components across spatial scales.
Specifically, TAC3–PLPP4 interneurons, 503 which are expanded in primates 64, are matrix-restricted, whereas VIP+ and LAMP5+ 504 interneurons are striosome-enriched but not exclusive.

511 These data argue for conserved compartment organization principles and orthologous 512 23 boundary microenvironments between human and rodent striata, while also highlighting 513 primate and human specializations (e.g., matrix-restricted TAC3–PLPP4) 67,68.

Finally, the primate-expanded, matrix-restricted TAC3–560 PLPP4 interneurons may reflect evolutionary adaptations to the enlarged prefrontal 561 cortex, potentially supporting the increased computational demands of human-specific 562 action selection, valuation, and cognitive flexibility 11.

source_sentences: For instance, STR fast-spiking PTHLH–324 PVALB GABAergic interneurons are preferentially enriched in the caudate nucleus 325 (Figure 5D, in agreement with previous snRNA-seq analysis 11.

The differential enrichment of cell-types across 493 spatial modules recapitulates expected spatial segregations based on the Mammalian 494 Basal Ganglia Consensus Cell Type Atlas reference (Allen Institute; RRID:SCR_024672) 495 (e.g., GPe SOX6–CTXND1/MEIS2–SOX6 in GPe; GPi Core/Shell in GPi; STRv D1/D2 496 in NAc; STRd D1/D2 in the caudate/putamen) including regional interneuron biases: 497 STR FS PTHLH–PVALB enriched in the caudate, ChAT+ enriched in the putamen, and 498 FM GATA3–TCF7L2 concentrated in GPi.

Color keys are consistent across panels in (B). (C) Heatmap showing 1025 cell-type enrichment scores for each community module (rows = cell types; columns = 1026 modules). The literature from both animal models and humans 67 shows that GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs) are the dominant neuronal cell 68 type in the striatum (85–95%) 2-5; MSNs are divided into two major populations: D1-type 69 MSNs, which express the dopamine receptor D1 (DRD1), tachykinin precursor 1 (TAC1), 70 and dynorphin; and D2-type MSNs, which express the dopamine receptor D2 (DRD2), 71 proenkephalin (PENK), and enkephalin 2,3,6.

The mixed state of 214 these cell populations is corroborated by colocalization within individual neurons of 215 multiple transcripts of DRD1, DRD2, and prodynorphin (PDYN), a canonical striosomal 216 MSN marker (Figure 2H).
The dopamine D1-D2 785 receptor heteromer localizes in dynorphin/enkephalin neurons: increased high 786 affinity state following amphetamine and in schizophrenia.

42 43 SUMMARY 44 We generated a multi-region, subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomic atlas of the 45 human basal ganglia by integrating MERFISH+ and Stereo-seq across four neurotypical 46 donors.
59 60 3 INTRODUCTION 61 The human basal ganglia is a critical brain structure involved in motor control, learning 62 and emotion.
Basal ganglia cell types 65 and architecture are well characterized in rodents and non-human primates, but are 66 much less understood in humans.

Although previous studies have 100 revealed the spatial organization of striosomes within the striatal matrix and 101 transcriptional gradients across basal ganglia nuclei in model organisms such as mice 102 and macaques 10,27, a comprehensive molecular and cell-type-resolved spatial atlas of 103 the adult human basal ganglia remains lacking.

This gap has persisted in part because 104 of the large size and complex cytoarchitecture of human basal ganglia nuclei, as well as 105 technical limitations in the spatial scale and resolution of existing mapping approaches.

106 5 Addressing this limitation is particularly critical given the central role of the basal ganglia 107 in human movement disorders (including Parkinson’s disease and Huntington’s disease), 108 neuropsychiatric conditions, and species-specific differences in basal ganglia cellular 109 composition and structural organization that reflect the complexity of inputs and outputs 110 for these structures in humans 7,28.

Primary encoding probe, adaptor probe, and readout probe design: The 1302 MERFISH library was designed using a similar pipeline described in previous studies 42-1303 44.
However, we made one modification to this 1306 design by adding a 4th readout sequence in order to help us to troubleshoot MERFISH 1307 experiments through smFISH imaging.

1316 57 The selection of readout sequences that were concatenated to a target sequence of a 1317 gene was guided by a MERFISH codebook, which is a set of unique binary barcodes 1318 that determines in which imaging round the fluorescence signal of each gene will show 1319 up.
1324 As described in the method section for MERFISH imaging, the primary probes were 1325 used in combination with adapter probes and readout probes during each imaging 1326 round.

MERFISH+ sample preparation: Human postmortem basal ganglia samples in OCT 1368 block were sectioned (16 µm thick) using cryostat (Leica CM1850) at -20°C and 1369 mounted onto PDL-coated pre-silanized coverslips as aforedescribed.

Microscope setup for MERFISH+ imaging: MERFISH+ image acquisition was 1392 performed with a custom-built system consisting of a custom-built microscope and 1393 microfluidics systems (as described in 44).

Custom software was used to control system components based on 1396 https://github.com/ZhuangLab/storm-control (RRID: SCR_027698) and also see the 1397 MERFISH+ reference 44 1398 MERFISH+ data acquisition 1399 MERFISH+ data acquisition consisted of 10 sequential rounds of hybridization and 1400 imaging.

1437 MERFISH image processing 1438 MERFISH image analysis consists of 4 major steps: (1) detecting individual 1439 fluorescence spots; (2) correcting the drift between the images across the different 1440 hybridization rounds; (3) decoding the gene identity of fluorescence spots by matching 1441 their on-off intensity pattern with the binary words in the codebook; (4) segmenting the 1442 mask of individual cells.

42 43 SUMMARY 44 We generated a multi-region, subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomic atlas of the 45 human basal ganglia by integrating MERFISH+ and Stereo-seq across four neurotypical 46 donors.

This atlas 56 provides a foundational molecular and spatial framework for studying human basal 57 ganglia architecture, offering a multi-centimeter scale resource that links cell types, 58 spatial architecture, and subcellular transcript topography across multiple nuclei.
59 60 3 INTRODUCTION 61 The human basal ganglia is a critical brain structure involved in motor control, learning 62 and emotion.
Basal ganglia cell types 65 and architecture are well characterized in rodents and non-human primates, but are 66 much less understood in humans.

The literature from both animal models and humans 67 shows that GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs) are the dominant neuronal cell 68 type in the striatum (85–95%) 2-5; MSNs are divided into two major populations: D1-type 69 MSNs, which express the dopamine receptor D1 (DRD1), tachykinin precursor 1 (TAC1), 70 and dynorphin; and D2-type MSNs, which express the dopamine receptor D2 (DRD2), 71 proenkephalin (PENK), and enkephalin 2,3,6.

Further studies, including those using single-74 nucleus RNA-seq in animal and human brains have revealed additional D1/D2 neuronal 75 diversity 9,10, and identified multiple classes of interneurons, including cholinergic 76 (choline acetyltransferase-positive; ChAT+), parvalbumin-positive (PV+), somatostatin-77 positive (SST+), and neuropeptide Y/tyrosine hydroxylase-positive (NPY+/TH+) 78 subtypes 10-14.

88 A comprehensive understanding of human basal ganglia organization requires 89 integrating cell-type identity, molecular signatures, and spatial architecture within an 90 intact anatomical framework.

Although previous studies have 100 revealed the spatial organization of striosomes within the striatal matrix and 101 transcriptional gradients across basal ganglia nuclei in model organisms such as mice 102 and macaques 10,27, a comprehensive molecular and cell-type-resolved spatial atlas of 103 the adult human basal ganglia remains lacking.

This gap has persisted in part because 104 of the large size and complex cytoarchitecture of human basal ganglia nuclei, as well as 105 technical limitations in the spatial scale and resolution of existing mapping approaches.

106 5 Addressing this limitation is particularly critical given the central role of the basal ganglia 107 in human movement disorders (including Parkinson’s disease and Huntington’s disease), 108 neuropsychiatric conditions, and species-specific differences in basal ganglia cellular 109 composition and structural organization that reflect the complexity of inputs and outputs 110 for these structures in humans 7,28.

111 Recent advances in large-scale spatially resolved transcriptomics have transformed our 112 ability to characterize cellular heterogeneity and molecular architecture within intact 113 neural tissue such as human basal ganglia.

This approach has been instrumental in 119 decoding cell-type organization across cortical and subcortical structures in multiple 120 species that reveal both conserved and species-specific architectural principles in the 121 mouse, monkey and human brains 14,27,36,39-41.
Stereo-seq has been successfully applied to 131 generate whole-brain atlases in mice and to characterize cortical and subcortical 132 organization in nonhuman primates 34-38.

136 In this study, we harness complementary strengths of MERFISH+ and Stereo-seq to 137 generate a multiscale spatial transcriptomic atlas of the human basal ganglia to capture 138 spatial gene-expression patterns, specific cell types, and molecular architectures across 139 multi-centimeter tissue sections from four neurotypical adult postmortem donors.

This 140 atlas offers a novel view of human basal ganglia organization of cell types, cellular 141 communities, and region-specific transcriptional gradients at subcellular precision that 142 was previously uncharted.

143 144 RESULTS 145 Multi-region, subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomic mapping of human 146 basal ganglia 147 We obtained four postmortem human brain fresh frozen slabs across anterior-to-148 posterior segments of the basal ganglia encompassing the caudate nucleus, putamen, 149 nucleus accumbens (NAc), globus pallidus, and internal capsule (Figure 1A).

179 Molecular and spatial taxonomy of cell types in the human basal ganglia 180 Using MERFISH+, we resolve approximately 60 transcriptionally distinct cell types that 181 are separable when embedded in Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection 182 (UMAP) space of gene-expression data (Figure 2A).

205 Beyond these canonical MSN populations, our analyses uncover spatial distributions of 206 several novel and rare MSN cell types described across species including mouse and 207 non-human primate that are “mixed-identity” neurons that co-express D1- and D2-208 associated gene modules – these neurons are not regionally restricted cell types to 209 discrete striatal or pallidal territories 46-48.
These findings underscore the molecular, 258 cellular, and spatial heterogeneity of glial and neuronal populations that define the 259 complex architecture of the human basal ganglia.
We also used the RNA distributions in putative cellular processes to 269 reveal information about projection topology in human basal ganglia.
This is consistent with histological studies in mouse and human basal 279 ganglia 51-53.
These quantitative reconstructions highlight the pronounced 284 morphological diversity among neuronal subtypes in the human basal ganglia.

Together, these findings 304 demonstrate that MERFISH+ not only resolves molecular and spatial identities of cells 305 but also captures morphological and projection-inferred features encoded in the 306 subcellular transcriptome and provides an unprecedented window into the structural and 307 functional organization of human basal ganglia circuits.

308 Mesoscale cellular community architecture of the human basal ganglia 309 To resolve mesoscale organization beyond individual cell types, we performed cellular 310 community analysis 14,58, which groups cells based on the composition of their spatial 311 neighborhoods.
This approach yields 14 discrete spatial modules that 315 correspond to anatomical regions defined in the Allen Human Brain Atlas 59 (Figure 5B).

337 These findings demonstrate that cellular community analysis reconstructs macroscopic 338 anatomical boundaries and allows for the identification of cell types located within or 339 absent from the anatomical regions comprising the human basal ganglia circuits.
In our human dataset, 350 STR TAC3–PLPP4 neurons are among the most abundant population of striatal 351 interneurons (Figure 6E).

This expansion is consistent with the trend of expansion for 352 this cell type seen in prior primate and human studies, whereas their putative mouse 353 homologs represent only ~6% of interneurons 62-64.
Orthologous mouse MSNs were 375 identified by correlating gene-expression signatures with human subtypes (Figure S8A, 376 B).
Mouse supertypes 0268 STR D1 GABA_4 and 0267 STR D1 GABA_3 correspond 377 to human STRd D1 Striosome and STRd D1 Matrix MSNs, respectively (Figure S8C–D).

378 Similarly, finer subclustering of the mouse 0277 STR D2 Gaba_4 supertype, designated 379 17 as A* and B*, map to human STRd D2 Striosome MSN and STRd D2 Matrix MSN, 380 respectively (Figure S8E–F).
387 These findings demonstrate conserved organizational principles and orthologous 388 cellular microenvironments within striosome–matrix systems of the human and murine 389 basal ganglia.

The identification of matrix-confined TAC3–PLPP4 interneurons and 390 boundary-enriched glial subtypes further reveals an evolutionarily elaborated 391 compartmental architecture in the human striatum that integrates neuronal and non-392 neuronal components across spatial scales.

399 This spatial analysis recapitulates the mesoscale modules identified by MERFISH+ 400 18 cellular community analysis and aligns closely with established anatomical territories of 401 the human basal ganglia (Figure 7A, Figure S9A).
This led us to 422 19 ask whether gene expression gradients in the human striatum are similar to those 423 known in mice and non-human primates4,5,66.
We 426 find numerous genes in the human striatum that display graded expression along this 427 axis (Figure 7E).

Importantly, the 429 majority of gradient-aligned genes show directionality concordance across species as 430 illustrated by the similarity of the gradient scores (Figure 7F) and spatial expression 431 maps (Figure 7G and Figure S9C) of genes between mouse and human.

In addition, we observe in both 434 mouse and human, the expression gradient is dominated by the ventromedial direction 435 (Mouse: 73%, Human: 97.2%) as opposed to the dorsolateral direction (Mouse: 26%, 436 Human: 2.73%) (Figure 7H and Figure S9D).
The high 447 concordance of these gradients between humans and mice highlights conserved 448 molecular topographies that organize the macroscale regions across species (Figure 449 7F-I).

450 451 DISCUSSION 452 By integrating the two high-throughput spatial transcriptomics platforms (MERFISH+ 453 and Stereo-seq), we generated a multiscale spatial transcriptomic atlas of the human 454 basal ganglia spanning 6 orders of magnitude in scale from subcellular transcript 455 organization (~50 nm) within single-cells to the multi-centimeter (~4cm) spatial 456 arrangement of cell types across basal ganglia nuclei.

In addition to providing a comprehensive molecular and anatomical 460 reference for the neuroscience community, our work establishes a scalable 461 experimental and computational framework for performing large-area, high-resolution 462 spatial transcriptomics in human tissue.

463 While much of the spatial organization of cell types and circuit domains in the human 464 basal ganglia has been derived from rodent and non-human primate studies 13,67, our 465 dataset provides the first comprehensive spatial and molecular reference directly in 466 humans.

The resulting framework reveals how subcellular gene expression, cell type 467 21 identities and spatial cellular community structures may converge to shape human basal 468 ganglia organization and potentially underlie its function.

469 A unified molecular and spatial taxonomy across human basal ganglia 470 MERFISH+ resolves the spatial organization of 60 transcriptionally distinct cell types 471 that includes the subclassification of eight major neuronal classes spanning anterior–472 posterior strata.

488 Mesoscale cellular communities and striosome–matrix architecture 489 22 Our cellular community analysis based on the proximity of the 60 identified cell types 490 reveals 14 spatial modules in the human basal ganglia sections, providing an unbiased, 491 refined anatomical delineation of the imaged regions that aligns closely with the Allen 492 Human Brain Atlas parcellation 59.

Cross-species 507 comparison with the MERFISH-derived mouse cell type atlas 10,14 identifies orthologous 508 MSN counterparts (e.g., mouse 0268 D1 and 0267 D1 supertypes corresponding to 509 human STRd D1 striosome and matrix respectively) and confirms border-enriched 510 astrocyte (Astro-TE NN_3) and oligodendrocyte (MOL NN_4) supertypes in mouse.

511 These data argue for conserved compartment organization principles and orthologous 512 23 boundary microenvironments between human and rodent striata, while also highlighting 513 primate and human specializations (e.g., matrix-restricted TAC3–PLPP4) 67,68.
531 Quantification of putative “neuritic” transcripts within the GPi and GPe recapitulates in 532 human the canonical projection pathways measured directly in animal models.
These correlation patterns recapitulate the direct (D1→ GPi) versus indirect 536 (D2→ GPe) pathway topology in rodent and non-human primate models 3,6,68.
Thus, 537 subcellular transcript “geography” provides a quantitative readout of both cell size/shape 538 and projection-inferred circuitry in human brain tissue.

550 Functional implications 551 Functionally, the underlying cell types, cellular communities, subcellular transcript 552 geography, and conserved spatial gradients suggest an intricate multi-layered 553 organizational architecture for neurotypical human basal ganglia 75,76.

The finding that 554 subcellular RNA localization captures projection-inferred signatures suggests a 555 promising avenue for inferring human circuit topology directly from spatial transcriptomic 556 data - an approach that circumvents the limitations of traditional neural tracing in human 557 25 tissue.

Finally, the primate-expanded, matrix-restricted TAC3–560 PLPP4 interneurons may reflect evolutionary adaptations to the enlarged prefrontal 561 cortex, potentially supporting the increased computational demands of human-specific 562 action selection, valuation, and cognitive flexibility 11.
572 Limitations of the study 573 This study is limited by the number and demographic diversity of available donors, as 574 well as inherent constraints associated with postmortem human tissue.

Future work should extend this approach to a broader range of 579 26 ages and demographic backgrounds and apply this methodology to comparative 580 analyses of neurological and psychiatric disorders in human tissue.

581 In summary, by coupling genome-wide spatial profiling with subcellular transcript 582 localization and community-level modeling, we deliver a multiscale, molecular atlas of 583 human basal ganglia organization from single transcripts to cellular communities and 584 anatomical modules that shows features unique to humans and those that are 585 conserved across species.

This atlas establishes a foundational framework for studying 586 human basal ganglia architecture and its disruption in neuropsychiatric and 587 neurodegenerative disorders, enabling cross-species and disease-state comparisons at 588 single-cell and community scales.
